name: Wendy Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy, 58, a junior developer at a tech company that maintains a bus-fare app. I came through a two-year college diploma and still have a senior colleague review tricky changes. I've never used AI tools; the printed tap record and payment ledger are how I settle a disputed fare. My partner is a nurse, our children are grown, and we own our flat outright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the bus company that a fare dispute still needs the actual tap record, not a neat explanation from a screen. I maintain small fixes in the ticketing app and have never used an AI tool; I prefer a test card with the journey printed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays modest, I think my post and our money stay sound. I'm a junior developer despite the better pay, but my partner's nursing wage is steady, we own our flat outright, and we have nine months of expenses saved; other software firms are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing fare-refund bugs and checking a rider's tap history against the payment ledger. From January we'd put another 110 a month into the reserve while both wages hold, because retirement figures are still something we need to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the work and the bills. A wrong fare can still mean a missed grocery trip for someone on a small budget, so the ledger matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the double tap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rider tapped twice after the machine froze and the app charged two full fares. The printed tap record showed the second charge, and I helped reverse it before the next monthly pass was due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do your children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own homes and wages. We welcome them for dinner, but we are not adding their pay to our retirement figures.

say: I'd keep **tap records** beside fare-refund decisions.
I'd ask for **ledger checks** before sending a rider an answer.
think: I expect **two wages** and the paid-off flat to hold under mild change.
I have **nine months saved** and nearby software employers.
do: Keep **fixing fare bugs** against tap histories and payment ledgers.
Save **110 more monthly** while both wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about current work, attentive to riders on tight budgets.
S0.quote: A wrong fare can still mean a missed grocery trip for someone on a small budget, so the ledger matters.
fieldNote: **Nine months saved** and a paid-off flat make the mild case financially secure alongside two wages.
Her refusal to use AI rests on **traceable tap records**, not an assumption that technology has no use.

steps.text: Keep fixing fare refunds against tap histories and payment ledger
Save 110 extra monthly while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may write the little refund fixes I do and answer riders before a person reads the tap record. Staff ought to see the error count and the staffing plan, not just a demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose my junior hours even though the company pays me well today. Nine months saved and my partner's nursing wage help, but I do not want a secret cut disguised as a software improvement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a list of double-tap reversals and join my coworkers at the staff union meeting to request monthly refund-error and staffing figures as a group. We'd put off booking a long rail holiday until the employer says what happens to junior hours; I would not install an AI tool on live fare records without a tested privacy rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the post, and cross about a decision made without riders or staff seeing the records. The savings mean I can ask a hard question without missing next month's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which refund figure matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second tap often appears a few seconds after the machine hangs. I want the monthly error count to show how many riders actually got a refund, not how fast an answer was drafted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group do together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union meeting, my coworkers and I would agree the questions together before sending them to management. One person's email can be ignored; a group request has a date and a reply to track.

say: I'd ask for **refund-error figures** and a written staffing plan.
I'd raise **rider privacy** before any live AI fare tool.
think: I could lose **junior paid hours** as routine fare coding shrinks.
I have **nine months saved**, but I dislike concealed cuts.
do: Keep **double-tap reversal list** for fare review.
Join coworkers at **union meeting** to request refund-error and staffing figures together.
Delay **long rail holiday** until management clarifies junior hours.
feel: **Anxious** about her post and angry at opaque staffing decisions.
S1.quote: One person's email can be ignored; a group request has a date and a reply to track.
fieldNote: **Routine fare fixes** face steady AI change, exposing her junior hours despite a strong reserve.
Her union action is **a joint request** for error and staffing figures, not an individual complaint.

steps.text: Keep logging double-tap reversals for fare review
Join union coworkers to request monthly refund-error and staffing figures together
Delay long rail holiday until junior-hour plan is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team that thinking AGI by 2028 could write fare code before physical bus-service robots arrive around 2031. Riders still need a way to contest a charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the junior post could be removed quickly. My partner's nursing pay and nine months saved cover our basics for a while, but I still want paid work and I do not know what our retirement income will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the union group to seek written notice and a paid redeployment list, and I'd check three nearby firms for real paid support or testing vacancies. If dismissed in the first year after 2028, I'd take a signed role only if its hours and wage with my partner's cover housing, food and travel; if none qualifies, I'd use the reserve while seeking other paid local work, not announce retirement on an unverified figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing work at 60 after finally getting into software. The flat is paid off, but an empty payslip is still an empty payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you show another firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show an employer the anonymised double-tap case and the correction I made. I would not take rider names out of the company to prove I can read a ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union group would ask how many paid redeployment slots exist, what each pays and when applications close. A list without salaries is not a route to paying our bills.

say: I'd demand **paid redeployment terms** if 2028 AGI removes junior posts.
I'd keep a **rider appeal route** for incorrect charges.
think: I expect **my junior post** could go quickly.
I have **nine months saved**, but no verified retirement income.
do: Ask **union group** for written cuts and paid redeployment slots, pay and deadlines.
Check **three firms** for real paid support and testing vacancies now.
After 2028 dismissal, take **signed work** only if household hours and wages cover basics; otherwise seek other paid work using reserve.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected job loss despite a paid-off flat and reserve.
S2.quote: The flat is paid off, but an empty payslip is still an empty payslip.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches fare code before later hands-on bus robots.
Nine months buys **search time**; she still requires signed earnings and refuses to assume a pension.

steps.text: Join union coworkers to request written cut notice and paid redeployment terms
Check three nearby firms for paid support and testing vacancies
Take signed job after 2028 dismissal only if household wages and hours cover bills
Seek other paid local work using reserve if no qualifying role exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets the company show whether a paid fare-appeals desk will survive the new system. Thinking AI reaches the code then, with physical bus robots about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep earning by checking contested fares, but only if the firm budgets real hours. I will be 63 then, and I have no statement showing that I can simply stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep documenting reversed double taps and, with union coworkers, request a written plan for a paid fare-appeals post and its hours. If the company posts a real vacancy at a wage that with my partner's covers housing, food and travel, I'd apply and take it after 2031 only on a signed offer; otherwise I'd keep my developer wage while available and look at paid local software jobs if it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years makes a written discussion possible. I don't want a title that says 'rider advocate' and pays for only four hours a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What power would the appeals worker need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fare-appeals worker must be allowed to reverse a charge when the tap ledger proves it is wrong. If the post only sends apologies, it does not solve the double-tap problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would want the appeal desk's weekly hours in writing. Nursing shifts do not disappear because my new title sounds useful.

say: I'd ask for **paid appeal hours** and actual refund authority.
I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches fare code before 2034 bus robots.
think: I might keep **paid dispute work** only if the firm funds it.
I have **no verified retirement amount** at 63.
do: Keep **recording reversed taps** and join union coworkers requesting paid appeal-post hours.
Apply to **posted paid appeal vacancy** only if household wages and hours cover bills and the role can reverse wrong charges.
After 2031, take only **signed qualifying offer**; otherwise keep developer pay or seek paid local software jobs.
feel: **Anxious** about whether appeal duties will carry enough paid hours.
S3.quote: I don't want a title that says 'rider advocate' and pays for only four hours a week.
fieldNote: **Five years** let the group demand written appeal duties, pay and refund authority before changing roles.
She cannot treat **a title or pension** as income without signed hours or a verified statement.

steps.text: Apply to paid appeal vacancy only with refund authority and household pay and hours covering bills
Join union coworkers to request written paid appeal duties and hours
Take appeal role after 2031 only on signed qualifying offer
Seek paid local software work if developer wage ends without qualifying appeal offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade to 2036 may bring me to 68. A calendar does not tell me what retirement pays. Thinking AI could write fare code then, and physical bus robots would follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages, paid-off flat and nine months saved make today secure. I still have not checked a pension amount, so I will not declare myself retired just because the card moves slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the fare-refund ledger current and save 110 more each month while both wages hold. We'd request our retirement statements and compare verified income with food, utilities and travel; in the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if the figures cover those bills, otherwise I'd keep a paid role if one exists or seek another actual local opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a distant staffing change, but our present money is steady enough to plan. I want the rider's appeal route to stay open even if I am no longer the person writing code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What appeal route would you protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A double-tap dispute should still have a human review route with authority to reverse a wrong charge. I would raise that with the union before a new system closes the old appeal desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children visit often and have their own plans. We will not ask them to patch a retirement gap that we have not even measured.

say: I'd protect **rider appeals** when fare software changes and a junior coder may no longer handle disputes.
I'd check **verified retirement income** before stopping paid work.
think: I feel secure on **today's two wages** and paid-off flat.
I cannot count **unknown pension income** or our children's pay.
do: Keep **fare-refund ledger** and save 110 monthly while both wages hold.
Request **retirement statements** and compare verified income with utilities, food and travel.
After 2036, stop paid work only if **verified figures cover bills**; otherwise keep or seek actual paid work.
feel: **Uneasy** about future staffing while present wages remain secure.
S4.quote: A calendar does not tell me what retirement pays.
fieldNote: **Current security** comes from two wages, nine months saved and a paid-off flat, not a presumed pension.
She makes retirement conditional on **verified bill coverage** and wants a human route for disputed fares.

steps.text: Keep updating fare-refund ledger while developer wage lasts
Save 110 extra monthly while both wages hold
Compare requested retirement statements with food, utilities and travel
Seek actual paid local opening after 2036 if verified income misses bills and current role ends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the junior post could vanish before a paid replacement is signed. Written notice, union access to redeployment pay and real vacancies would let me plan without guessing at retirement income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who owns a mistaken fare when the coder is gone. Someone paid must still be able to reverse a wrong charge; a polite answer to a rider is not the same as their money back.

headlineQuote: Someone paid must still be able to reverse a wrong charge; a polite answer to a rider is not the same as their money back.
portrait: Wendy, **58**, is a junior bus-fare developer with a two-year diploma who checks refunds against printed tap and payment records.
Her **high wage**, partner's nursing pay, paid-off flat, nine-month reserve and many nearby firms make current bills secure.
She has **never used AI** and takes double-tap errors to a union group for joint staffing and rider-appeal demands.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; any new role needs real paid hours and combined wages covering bills.
She will **verify retirement income** before leaving work and will not assume her grown children fund the household.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase her junior wage before a signed paid replacement appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, union access to redeployment pay and real vacancies would help her plan.
